Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 1:

﴿Their reckoning has drawn near for mankind﴾. "Mankind" (al-nas) is a general term. Ibn ʿAbbas said that what is meant here is specifically the polytheists of Quraysh, as evidenced by what follows, since it describes their attributes. He described the Hour as near because what has passed of time before it is greater than what remains of it, and because everything that is coming is near.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 2–4:

﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord, newly revealed﴾. By "reminder" (dhikr) is meant the Qur'an, and "newly revealed" (muhdath) means newly sent down.

﴿And they conspire in secret, those who did wrong﴾. The waw in ﴿wa-asarru﴾ is the subject pronoun (damir) referring to what precedes it. ﴿Alladhina zalamu﴾ is a substitution (badal) for that pronoun. It was also said that the subject is ﴿alladhina zalamu﴾ itself, and this is found in the dialect of those who say *akaluni al-baraghith* (the fleas ate me), which is the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b. Sibawayh said: "This dialect does not occur in the Qur'an." It is possible that ﴿alladhina zalamu﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, expressing disapproval, or is the predicate of an implied subject, but the first view is better.

﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ This statement is in the accusative position as a substitution (badal) for "the secret talk," because it is the words they conspired with. The "human being" mentioned in the verse is our master Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿He said: My Lord knows the word﴾. This is information that what they conspired with, they kept secret. If it is asked: why did He not say "knows the secret," in keeping with His saying ﴿and they conspire in secret﴾? The answer: "the word" (qawl) includes both the secret and the open, so mention of the secret is achieved along with something more.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 5–6:

﴿Nay, they say: "A confusion of dreams."﴾ That is, a mixture of dream-visions. He related many of their statements to show the confusion of their affair and the falsehood of their sayings. ﴿As the earlier ones were sent [with signs].﴾ That is, just as the earlier messengers came with signs, so let Muhammad bring us a sign. The comparison is therefore in the bringing of a miracle. ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed.﴾ When they said: ﴿Let him bring us a sign,﴾ God informed them that those before them had asked for signs, and when they saw them and did not believe, they were destroyed. Then He said: ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ That is, their state in not believing and in destruction is like the state of those before them. It is also possible that the meaning is: every town that was destroyed did not believe, so these too are like that; and on this reading it is not an answer to their saying ﴿Let him bring us a sign,﴾ but rather a fresh statement in the form of a threat. And ﴿We destroyed it﴾ is in the position of a descriptive clause for ﴿town﴾, and what is meant is the people of the town.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 11–13:

﴿قَصَمْنَا﴾ means "We destroyed," and its root is from "qasm al-zahr," meaning to break the back. ﴿مِن قَرْيَةٍ﴾ means "the people of a town." Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is a town in Yemen called Ḥuḍūr. God sent to them a prophet, and they killed him, so God set over them Bukhtnasar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Babylon, who destroyed them by killing. The apparent wording is general, because kam (how many) denotes multiplicity, so it does not refer to one specific town. ﴿يَرْكُضُونَ﴾ is an expression for their fleeing. It may be that they mounted animals and spurred them to make them run faster, or that their swift running on foot was likened to one who spurs a mount. ﴿لاَ تَرْكُضُواْ﴾ means that it was said to them, "Do not flee." The speakers of this were the angels, saying it to mock them; or, if the town in question is the specific one, Bukhtnasar's men said it to them as deception, so that they would return and be killed. ﴿أُتْرِفْتُمْ﴾ means "you were given luxury." ﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تُسْأَلُونَ﴾ is mockery and rebuke: that is, "Return to your luxury and your dwellings, perhaps you will be asked about what befell you." It may also be that ﴿تُسْأَلُونَ﴾ means that people will seek your favours, and this too is mockery.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 14–16:

﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ The verse is an acknowledgment and regret, when it no longer benefited them. ﴿Cut down, extinguished﴾: they were likened in their destruction to a harvested crop. The meaning of ﴿extinguished﴾ is dead, and it is a comparison with the extinguishing of a fire. ﴿In play﴾ is a negated circumstantial clause, meaning: We did not create the heavens and the earth for the sake of play, but for reflection upon them and for drawing inference from them to their Creator.

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 21, verses 17–21:**

﴿If We had wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence﴾. *Al-lahw* (pastime) in the dialect of Yemen means a child, and it is said that it means a woman. ﴿From Our presence﴾ means from the angels. On this reading the meaning is: if We had wished to take a child, We would have taken one from the angels, not from the children of Adam. This is a refutation of those who said that the Messiah is the son of God and that Uzayr is the son of God. The apparent meaning, however, is that *al-lahw* means play, since it is connected to His words "playing" (*la'ibin*).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning on this reading is that if We had wished to take a pastime, that would have been within Our power, but it does not befit Us, because it contradicts wisdom. There is room for scrutiny in both views. ﴿If We were doers﴾: *in* (if) may be a conditional particle, whose answer is in what precedes it, or it may be a negative particle. The first is more evident. ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood﴾. *Al-haqq* (the truth) is general: it covers the Qur'an, the message, the law, and everything that is true. *Al-batil* (falsehood) is general too, covering the opposites of these. ﴿So it crushes it﴾: that is, it suppresses it and nullifies it. Its root is from striking the brain (*dimagh*). ﴿And those who are with Him﴾ means the angels. ﴿And they do not tire﴾: that is, they do not grow weary and do not become bored.

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who can raise the dead?﴾ Here *am* (or) is used for transition (*idrab*) away from what precedes it, and the interrogation (*istifham*) is in the form of rejection (*inkar*) of what follows it. The phrase ﴿from the earth﴾ is connected to "raise" (*yunshirun*). The meaning is: the gods the polytheists have taken cannot raise the dead from the earth, so they are not gods in reality, for one of the attributes of a god is the power to give life and to cause death.

﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted.﴾ This is a proof of the oneness of Allah, the Exalted. The pronoun in His words ﴿in them﴾ refers to the heavens and the earth. The phrase ﴿other than Allah﴾ is a qualifier of "gods," and "other than" (illa) here means "ghayr" (other than). The statement therefore implies two matters. The first is the negation of a plurality of gods, and the necessity that the god be one. The second is that this one is Allah and not another. The second matter is indicated by His words ﴿other than Allah﴾. As for the first, the verse would indicate it even without this phrase. Many people have said concerning the meaning of the verse that it is evidence for the argument from mutual exclusion (al-tamanu', the argument of mutual prevention) that the usul scholars (the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence) have presented. This is that if we suppose two gods, and one of them wills something while the other wills its opposite, then either the will of each of them is executed, which is impossible because two contradictories cannot coexist; or the will of neither of them is executed, which is also impossible, because two contradictories cannot both be negated, and because that leads to their incapacity and deficiency, so that they would not be gods; or the will of one of them is executed and not the will of the other. Then the one whose will is executed is the god, and the one whose will is not executed is not a god, so the god is one. Even if we grant the soundness of this proof, the wording of the verse does not correspond to it. Rather, the apparent sense of the wording points to another argument that is more sound than the argument from mutual exclusion, namely that if there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both be corrupted, because of the disagreement and dispute that would arise between them over management and the intention of dominating one another. Do you not see that there are not two kings for one city, nor two governors for one district? ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ because He is the owner of everything, and the owner acts in his own property as he wishes; and because He is wise, so all His actions proceed according to wisdom. ﴿But they will be questioned﴾, for the absence of the two causes. ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ He repeated this denunciation to magnify shirk and to exaggerate its ugliness, because before it were attributes of Allah that require His oneness, and in order to attach to it what is mentioned after it, namely the rebuke of the polytheists and the fact that they have no proof for their shirk, neither from the standpoint of reason nor from the standpoint of revelation (al-shar').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 30–31:

﴿They were a closed-up mass, then We parted them⦆ Al-ratq (closed-up mass) is a verbal noun used as a descriptive, and its meaning is that which is joined together, one part to another, with no crack in it and no opening. Al-fatq (parting) is opening. It was said: the heavens were joined to the earth, and Allah parted them by the air. It was also said: the heavens were joined one to another, and the earths likewise, and Allah parted them, seven by seven. On this view, the seeing in His words ﴿Have they not seen?﴾ is seeing of the heart (intellectual perception). It was also said: He parted the sky by rain and the earth by vegetation, and on this view the seeing is seeing of the eye.

﴿And We made from water every living thing⦆ That is, We created from water every animal, and by water is meant the seminal fluid. It was also said: the water that is drunk, because it is the cause of the life of animals, and vegetation enters into this by metaphor. ﴿Firm mountains⦆ means the mountains. ﴿Lest it should shake⦆ its estimated sense is "out of aversion that it should shake." ﴿Broad roads⦆ means the great paths. Its grammatical analysis according to al-Zamakhshari is that it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of "paths," because it is a descriptive that preceded the indefinite noun. ﴿That perhaps they may be guided⦆ means in their way and their conduct.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 32–33:

﴿a protected roof﴾: meaning, protected from falling and from the devils. ﴿Yet from its signs they turn away﴾: meaning the stars, the rains, the thunder, the lightning and other such things. ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾: the tanwin in ﴿kullun﴾ (each) is a substitute for the idafa (the genitive construction), meaning: all of them are swimming in an orbit, that is, the sun and the moon, but not the night and the day, since night and day are not described as swimming in an orbit. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the sun and the moon, or it is a new independent clause (mustanaf). If it is asked: the word kull and the verb yasbahun are plural, so how can it mean the sun and the moon when they are two? The answer: it intends the category of their risings, each day and night, and these are many; this is said by al-Zamakhshari. Al-Qazwini said: it intends the sun, the moon and all the wandering stars, and he referred to them with the plural pronoun used for rational beings in His words ﴿yasbahun (they swim)﴾, because He described them with an action of rational beings, which is swimming. If it is asked: how does He say "in an orbit" (falak), when there are many orbits? The answer: He intends that each one swims in its own orbit. This is like the saying "the amir clothed them with a robe," meaning he clothed each one of them with a robe. The meaning of falak is a rounded body. Some of the exegetes said it is made of waves, but that is far-fetched. The truth is that its nature and mode are not known except through a sound report from the Lawgiver (al-Shari'), and that is not available. The meaning of yasbahun is they run, or they revolve, and it is borrowed from sabh (swimming) in the sense of floating in water. And His words ﴿kullun fi falakin (each in an orbit)﴾ are from the inverted construction (al-maqlub) which can be read from both ends.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 34:

﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity.﴾ Its occasion (sabab) is that the disbelievers criticised the Prophet ﷺ, saying he was a human who would die. It is also said that they wished for his death so that they could gloat over him, and this is more fitting with what follows it. ﴿Then if you die, will they be the ones who live forever?﴾ The place of the interrogative hamza (ʾa-, the hamzat al-istifham) is after the fa', so that it reads "fa-hum al-khalidun" (then they are the eternal ones), but it has been moved forward because interrogation (al-istifham) has precedence at the head of the sentence (sadr al-kalam).

Every soul shall taste death (dhā'iqat al-mawt). That is, every created soul must taste death, and "taste" (al-dhawq) here is a metaphor. "And We test you with evil and with good" (wa-nablūkum bi-l-sharri wa-l-khayr): that is, We try you with poverty and wealth, health and sickness, and other circumstances of this world, so that patience in evil and gratitude for good may become manifest, or the opposite of that. "As a trial" (fitnatan): a verbal noun (maṣdar) derived from the sense of "We test you."

ۣThis is the face-value rendering of the passage as given.

﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods﴾ meaning, speaks of them disparagingly. The context indicates this, for mentioning (dhikr) can be either with blame or with praise. The clause is an explanation of the mockery, i.e., they say: "Is this the one who ...". ﴿while they are disbelievers in the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: how do they deny your condemnation of their gods while they themselves disbelieve in the Most Merciful? Thus they are more deserving of blame. It has also been said: the meaning of "the remembrance of the Most Merciful" is naming Him with this name, because they denied it. The first explanation is more profound in showing their misguidance.

﴿Man was created of haste.﴾ That is, he was created very hasty. This expression is used for emphasis (al-mubalagha, hyperbole), as in their saying: "He was created from generosity," referring to Hatim. "Man" here is a generic term for mankind. The occasion of revelation was that the disbelievers demanded hasty answers to the signs they had proposed and hastened the punishment they had asked for. God mentioned this as a preface (tawti'a) to His words: ﴿So do not ask Me to hasten.﴾ It is also said that the intended meaning is Adam, because when the spirit reached his chest he wanted to stand up. But this view is weak. It is also said that ﴿of haste﴾ means "of clay," but this is weaker. ﴿I will show you My signs﴾ is a threat and a response to what they asked for in terms of hastening. ﴿And they say﴾ and the verse that follows explains their hastening. ﴿The promise﴾ refers to the Resurrection. It is also said that it refers to the descent of the punishment upon them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 42:

﴿Who can protect you﴾ means: who can guard you from the command of Allah? The word "man" (who) is interrogative (istifhamiyyah), and the meaning is a threat and the establishment of proof, because if they answered this question they would have to acknowledge that they have no defender and no protector. Then His words ﴿Nay, they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾ mean that when they are asked this question they do not answer it, because the proof would be established against them if they answered. Rather, they turn away from the remembrance of Allah: that is, from the answer that contains the remembrance of Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of the "idrab" (change of direction, "nay/rather") here is that they turn away from His remembrance, let alone that they fear His punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 43:

﴿Or do they have gods that can protect them from Us?﴾ That is, that can protect them from the punishment. Here "am" (or) is interrogative, and its meaning is denial and negation. This is because when He asked them about who could guard them, He then informed them that their gods cannot protect them or keep them safe, and then He argued for this by His saying: ﴿They are not able to help themselves﴾, for whoever cannot help himself is more deserving of not being able to help others. ﴿Nor will they be accompanied by Us (in protection)﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning they will not be accompanied by any help or protection from Us.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 44–48:

﴿Nay, We gave enjoyment to these people﴾ — meaning, We gave them enjoyment of blessings and well-being in this world, so they transgressed because of it and forgot the punishment of God. The turn with "bal" (nay/rather) is a shift away from the meaning of the preceding statement: that is, neither victory nor protection prevented them from disbelief and mockery; rather, what drove them to that was that We gave enjoyment to them and to their fathers.

﴿We reduce it from its edges﴾ — mentioned in Surah al-Ra'd [13:43]. ﴿Nor do the deaf hear the call﴾ — an indication of the disbelievers, and "the deaf" is a metaphor for their extreme aversion. ﴿A breath﴾ — that is, a passing touch; it implies a lessening of the punishment, and the meaning is that if they saw even the least thing of God's punishment, they would submit and acknowledge their sins. ﴿And We set up the scales of justice﴾ — that is, the justice. The word "qist" (justice) is singular though it describes a plural, because it is a verbal noun used as an attribute, like "'adl" (justice) and "rida" (contentment), or with the implied sense of "possessors of justice." The doctrine of the People of the Sunna is that the scale on the Day of Resurrection is real, having two pans, a tongue, and a beam on which deeds are weighed; lightness and heaviness pertain to bodies, whether the scrolls of deeds or whatever God wills. The Mu'tazila said that the scale is a metaphor for justice in recompense. ﴿For the Day of Resurrection﴾ — Ibn 'Atiyya said its estimated meaning is: "for the reckoning of the Day of Resurrection, or for wisdom," so it contains an elided genitive. al-Zamakhshari said it is like your saying, "I wrote the book for six nights remaining of the month." ﴿The weight of a mustard seed﴾ — that is, its weight. The nominative is when "kana" is complete (taamma), and the accusative is when it is incomplete (naqisa) with an implied subject. ﴿The Criterion﴾ — here it refers to the Torah. It was also said it means the distinction between truth and falsehood through victory and the establishment of proof.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 55–61:

﴿They said: "Have you brought us the truth, or are you among those who jest?"﴾ That is, is what you say true, or is it mere jest? Observe how he expressed "the truth" with a verbal form, and "play" with a nominal sentence, because it is more firmly established in their eyes. ﴿"He Who originated them"﴾ That is, Who created them, and the pronoun refers to the heavens and the earth, or to the statues. The latter is more fitting for refuting them. ﴿"after you have turned away, retreating"﴾ That is, after they had gone out to their festival. ﴿"into fragments"﴾ That is, into small pieces. It may be read with a ḍammah, a kasrah, or a fatḥah, and it derives from al-jadhdh (jadh, meaning "cutting"). ﴿"except a large one among them"﴾ He left the large idol unbroken and hung the axe around its neck. ﴿"so that they may return to it"﴾ The pronoun refers to the large idol, meaning that they may return to it, ask it, and it will not answer them, so it becomes evident to them that it has no power over anything. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, meaning that they may return to him and he will explain the truth to them.

﴿They said: "Who has done this to our gods?"﴾ Before it there is an omitted element, its sense being: they returned from their festival and saw the idols broken, and they said: ﴿"Who has done this?"﴾ ﴿"A youth who speaks of them"﴾ That is, who mentions them with blame and with his saying: ﴿"By Allah, I will surely plot against your idols"﴾. ﴿"who is called Ibrahim"﴾ It has been said that the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of Ibrahim is as a vocative (munada); it has been said that it is the predicate of an implied subject; it has been said that it is in the nominative by way of al-ihmal (leaving it unanalysed). The sound view is that it is the object of a verb whose subject is not named, because what is meant is the name, not the one named; this is the choice of Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari. ﴿"so that they may bear witness"﴾ That is, they may bear witness against him for what he did, or they may attend his punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 64–65:

It is possible that ﴿they were turned upside down upon their heads﴾ means their return from argument to silence, for their saying ﴿"You surely know that these do not speak"﴾ is an admission that entails that they have been overcome by the proof. It is also possible, on this reading, that ﴿they were turned upside down upon their heads﴾ is literal: that is, they lowered their heads out of shame, since the proof had been established against them.

The word ḥarth (field) is used for both. ﴿When the sheep of certain people grazed in it by night﴾ (nafashat: it grazed in it at night). ﴿And We were witness to their judgment﴾. The pronoun refers to Dawud, Sulayman and the litigants. It was also said that it refers to Dawud and Sulayman alone, on the basis that the least number of a plural is two. ﴿So We gave the understanding of it to Sulayman﴾. Two men brought a dispute before Dawud: the sheep of one of them had entered the field of the other at night and damaged it. Dawud ruled that the owner of the field should take the sheep. The reasoning behind this ruling was that the value of the crop was equal to the value of the sheep. The two men went out and met Sulayman, who was at the gate, and they informed him of what his father had ruled. He entered to his father and said: "O Prophet of God, had you judged otherwise, it would have been kinder to all." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "The owner of the sheep should take the land to cultivate it until its crop returns as it was, and the owner of the crop should take the sheep and benefit from their milk, wool and offspring. When the crop is complete, the sheep are returned to their owner and the land with its crop to its owner." Dawud said to him: "You have been granted success, my son," and he judged between them accordingly. The rationale of Sulayman's judgment is that he made the benefit from the sheep correspond to what was lost of the crop, and it is obligatory for the owner of the sheep to work in the field until the harm and deficiency are removed. It is possible that this was an act of reconciliation rather than a judgment.

It is narrated that Dawud retracted his judgment when it became clear to him that the correct ruling was otherwise. Whoever said it was by revelation made Sulayman's judgment abrogating (naskh) Dawud's judgment.

Abu Hanifa said: the owner is not liable for what they damage either at night or during the day, on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The injury caused by an animal is unaccountable (jubar)."

﴿And We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. It was said: this refers to this particular case, and that Dawud did not err in it, but rather returned to what was more correct; this view is supported by the principle that every mujtahid is correct. It was also said: rather, it means judgment and knowledge in other than this case, and on this view he erred in it, and the correct one is one of the mujtahids. ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify with Dawud, and the birds﴾. This glorification was saying "Subhan Allah." It was also said: it means prayer with him when he prayed. The mountains were mentioned before the birds because their glorification is more remarkable, since they are inanimate. ﴿And We were ever doing﴾, i.e., able to do this.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is that this was in his regard because Dawud deserved it in equal share... [as stated]. ﴿The making of coats of mail﴾, i.e., iron armor, and the first to make them was Dawud, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Atiyya said that linguistically labus means weapons, while al-Zamakhshari said labus means garment. ﴿That it may protect you from your violence﴾, i.e., to shield you in battle. It is read with the letters ya', ta' and nun: the nun refers to God Most High, the ta' to the craft, and the ya' to Dawud or to the armor. ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ The wording is interrogative, but its meaning is an invitation to gratitude. ﴿And to Sulayman the wind, violently blowing﴾. It was also said: it would blow strongly when he raised the carpet and become gentle when it carried him. ﴿To the land which We had blessed﴾, meaning the land of Syria, which was his dwelling and the seat of his rule; the return to it was specified in the verse because it implies departure from it. ﴿And of the devils, those who dove for him﴾, i.e., they entered the water to extract jewels for him from the seas. ﴿And other work beside that﴾, less than diving, such as construction and service. ﴿And We were a guardian over them﴾, i.e., We guarded them from deviating from his command, or from spoiling what they made. Two men brought a dispute before Dawud: the sheep of one of them had entered the field of the other at night and damaged it. Dawud ruled that the owner of the field should take the sheep. The reasoning behind this ruling was that the value of the crop was equal to the value of the sheep. The two men went out and met Sulayman, who was at the gate, and they informed him of what his father had ruled. He entered to his father and said: "O Prophet of God, had you judged otherwise, it would have been kinder to all." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "The owner of the sheep should take the land to cultivate it until its crop returns as it was, and the owner of the crop should take the sheep and benefit from their milk, wool and offspring. When the crop is complete, the sheep are returned to their owner and the land with its crop to its owner." Dawud said to him: "You have been granted success, my son," and he judged between them accordingly. The rationale of Sulayman's judgment is that he made the benefit from the sheep correspond to what was lost of the crop, and it is obligatory for the owner of the sheep to work in the field until the harm and deficiency are removed. It is possible that this was an act of reconciliation rather than a judgment.

People differed as to whether their judgment was by revelation or by ijtihad (independent reasoning). Whoever said it was by ijtihad permitted ijtihad for the prophets. It is narrated that Dawud retracted his judgment when it became clear to him that the correct ruling was otherwise. Whoever said it was by revelation made Sulayman's judgment abrogating (naskh) Dawud's judgment.

Abu Hanifa said: the owner is not liable for what they damage either at night or during the day, on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The injury caused by an animal is unaccountable (jubar)."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 83–84:

﴿And Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord﴾ Ayyub (peace be upon him) was a prophet from the Romans, and it is said he was from the Children of Israel. He had children and abundant wealth, and God took away his wealth and he was patient. Then He took away his children and he was patient. Then He afflicted his body with illness and he was patient, until his people passed by him and mocked him. At that point he called upon God Most High. As for his saying: ﴿Harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, it is not an explicit supplication, but rather he mentioned his own state in a way that calls for mercy, and described his Lord with the utmost mercy so that He would show mercy to him. In this there is a kind of gentle courtesy that is absent in an explicit request. ﴿So We removed what was with him of harm﴾. When God answered him, He caused a spring of water to gush forth for him, and he drank from it and bathed, and he was cured of the illness and affliction. ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. It is related that God restored his children who had died and granted him their like along with them in this world. It is also said: in the Hereafter. It is also said: his wife bore children equal in number to his dead children, and their like along with them. God also compensated him with more than what he had lost of his wealth. ﴿As a mercy from Us﴾, that is, a mercy to Ayyub, and a reminder to others among the worshippers, that they may be patient as he was patient. It is also possible that the mercy and the reminder are both for the worshippers.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 87–88:

﴿وَذَا ٱلنُّونِ﴾ is Yunus (peace be upon him), and al-Nun is the fish (al-hut), so called because it swallowed him. ﴿إِذ ذَّهَبَ مُغَاضِباً﴾ means angry with his people, since he had been calling them to God and they disbelieved, until weariness with them overcame him and he left them. This is why God said: ﴿وَلاَ تَكُن كَصَاحِبِ ٱلْحُوتِ﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] ("Be not like the companion of the fish"). The view of those who say he was angry with his Lord is not sound. ﴿فَظَنَّ أَن لَّن نَّقْدِرَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ means he thought that We would not constrict (lan naqdira) upon him. This is from the same sense as the phrase "qadara 'alayhi rizqahu" (He restricted his provision). It is also said that it derives from qadar (decree) and qada' (judgment), meaning he thought that We would not constrict upon him by punishment. The view of those who say it derives from qudrah (power) is not sound. ﴿فَنَادَىٰ فِي ٱلظُّلُمَاتِ﴾ It is said that this statement is elided, since it is explained in another verse, namely that when he left he boarded a ship, was thrown into the sea, and the fish swallowed him; then ﴿فَنَادَىٰ فِي ٱلظُّلُمَاتِ﴾. The "darknesses" are the darkness of the night, of the sea, and of the belly of the fish. It is also possible that "darkness" is used figuratively for the belly of the fish because of its intense darkness, as in God's words: ﴿وَتَرَكَهُمْ فِي ظُلُمَاتٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] ("and left them in darknesses"). ﴿أَن لاَّ إِلَـٰهَ إِلاَّ أَنتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّالِمِينَ﴾ "an" here is either explanatory (mufassirah) or verbal-source (masdariyyah), on the reading that he called out "bi-an" (with the words). This is why the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The supplication of my brother Yunus, Dhu'l-Nun: no distressed person has ever made it except that it was answered for him."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 95:

﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return.﴾ It is recited as "ḥirm" (حِرْم) with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, and it has the same meaning as "ḥarām" (حرام). The scholars differed about the meaning of the verse. It was said: "ḥarām" means "prohibited," so the sense is that a town which God intended to destroy is prohibited from returning to God in repentance, or a town which God destroyed is prohibited from returning to the world. Here "lā" (لا) is extra (zāʾida, meaning superfluous or redundant) in both interpretations. It was also said: "ḥarām" means "a decree (ḥatm, حتم) that is certain to occur," and both interpretations can be understood from it, with "lā" being a negation in both. That is, the decree is that they will not return to God in repentance, or the decree is that they will not return to the world. It was said: the meaning is that a town which God destroyed is prohibited from their returning to Him in the Hereafter. Here "lā" is also a negation, and this contains a refutation of those who deny the resurrection.

**Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on 21:96–98**

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾. Here *hatta* (ḥattā) is a *ḥarf ibtidā'* (a particle marking a beginning) or a *ghāya* (a limit or end point), connected to *yarji'ūn* (they return). The answer to *idhā* (when) is *fa-idhā hiya shākhiṣa* (then, behold, the eyes will stare fixedly). It was also said that the answer is *yā waylanā* (O woe to us), since the implied sense is "they will say, O woe to us." *Futiḥat Yājūj wa-Mājūj* means the opening of their barrier, so the noun that was annexed (*al-muḍāf*, the word that was dropped) has been omitted.

﴿And they will swarm from every *ḥadab* (elevated ground)﴾. *Al-ḥadab* is the raised part of the earth. *Yansilūn* means they will hasten. The pronoun refers to Gog and Magog, meaning they will come out from every path because of their great numbers. It was also said that it refers to all of mankind.

﴿The true promise﴾: this means the Resurrection.

﴿Then, behold, they will stare fixedly﴾. Here *idhā* is *idhā lil-mufājaʾa* (*idhā* of sudden surprise). The pronoun (*ḍamīr*) is, according to Sibawayh, *ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa* (a pronoun referring to the matter or event itself). According to al-Farrāʾ, it refers to the eyes (*al-abṣār*). *Shākhiṣa* derives from *shukhūṣ*, which is the fixed staring of the eyes out of fear.

﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides God, are *ḥaṣab* (fuel) for Hell﴾. This is addressed to the polytheists. *Al-ḥaṣab* is that with which a fire is kindled, like firewood (*al-ḥaṭab*). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) read *ḥaṭab Jahannam*. What is meant by "what you worship" is the idols and other things, which will be burned in the Fire as a rebuke to those who worshipped them.

﴿*Wāridūn*﴾: *al-wurūd* here means entering.

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾. Here *hatta* (ḥattā) is a *ḥarf ibtidā'* (a particle marking a beginning) or a *ghāya* (a limit or end point), connected to *yarji'ūn* (they return). The answer to *idhā* (when) is *fa-idhā hiya shākhiṣa* (then, behold, the eyes will stare fixedly). It was also said that the answer is *yā waylanā* (O woe to us), since the implied sense is "they will say, O woe to us." *Futiḥat Yājūj wa-Mājūj* means the opening of their barrier, so the noun that was annexed (*al-muḍāf*, the word that was dropped) has been omitted.

﴿And they will swarm from every *ḥadab* (elevated ground)﴾. *Al-ḥadab* is the raised part of the earth. *Yansilūn* means they will hasten. The pronoun refers to Gog and Magog, meaning they will come out from every path because of their great numbers. It was also said that it refers to all of mankind.

﴿The true promise﴾: this means the Resurrection.

﴿Then, behold, they will stare fixedly﴾. Here *idhā* is *idhā lil-mufājaʾa* (*idhā* of sudden surprise). The pronoun (*ḍamīr*) is, according to Sibawayh, *ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa* (a pronoun referring to the matter or event itself). According to al-Farrāʾ, it refers to the eyes (*al-abṣār*). *Shākhiṣa* derives from *shukhūṣ*, which is the fixed staring of the eyes out of fear.

﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides God, are *ḥaṣab* (fuel) for Hell﴾. This is addressed to the polytheists. *Al-ḥaṣab* is that with which a fire is kindled, like firewood (*al-ḥaṭab*). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) read *ḥaṭab Jahannam*. What is meant by "what you worship" is the idols and other things, which will be burned in the Fire as a rebuke to those who worshipped them.

﴿*Wāridūn*﴾: *al-wurūd* here means entering.

﴿زَفِيرٌ﴾ [a groaning, a loud exhaled sigh], mentioned in Hud, and ﴿لاَ يَسْمَعُونَ﴾ [they will not hear].

It was said: they will be placed in coffins (tawabit) of fire, so they will not hear anything. It was also said: Allah will deafen them just as He blinds them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 101–104:

﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us﴾. "Sabaqat" means: it was decreed in eternity (al-azal). "Al-husna" means happiness. The verse was revealed when Ibn al-Zib'ari objected to His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [21:98]. He said: "Isa, Uzayr and the angels have been worshipped." The meaning is that these are excluded from that threat, though the wording remains general for everyone for whom happiness has preceded.

﴿Its faint sound﴾: its sound. ﴿The greatest terror﴾: the horrors of the Resurrection in general. It was also said that it is the slaughter of death, and it was said that it is the first blast of the Trumpet, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾ [27:87].

﴿Like the folding of the scroll for the records﴾. "Al-sijill" means the sheet, and "al-kitab" is a verbal noun. The meaning is: as the scroll is folded so that something may be written in it, or so that the book in it may be preserved. It was also said that "al-sijill" is a scribe, but this is weak. It was also said that it is an angel in the second heaven to whom deeds are raised, and this too is weak.

﴿As We initiated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾. The meaning is: as We were able to originate creation, We are able to restore it. This is like His saying: ﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time﴾ [36:79]. It was also said that the meaning is that We will restore them in the form in which We originated them, as in the hadith: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised." Then he (ﷺ) recited: ﴿As We initiated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾. The particle "ka" (like) is connected to His saying "nu'iduhu" (We will repeat it).

﴿Doers﴾: as an emphasis on the certainty of the Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verse 105:

﴿And We had certainly written in the Zabur (the Psalms) after the Dhikr (the Remembrance).﴾ There are two opinions regarding "the Zabur" here. The first is that it is the Book of Dawud (David). On this view, "the Dhikr" is the Tawrah (Torah) that Allah sent down to Musa (Moses), together with what the Zabur contains of the mention of Allah, the Exalted. The second opinion is that "the Zabur" is a general term for the books that Allah sent down to all the Prophets. On this view, "the Dhikr" is the Lawh al-Mahfuz (the Preserved Tablet). That is, Allah wrote this in the Book set apart for it, after He had written it in the Preserved Tablet and decreed all matters. The first opinion is more correct, because applying the term "Zabur" to the Book of Dawud is clearer and more common in usage. Also, "Zabur" is singular, so indicating a single book is more correct than indicating a collection. Moreover, the text has been reported in the Zabur of Dawud that the earth will be inherited by the righteous: ﴿that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾. Here, "the earth" is unrestricted, covering the eastern and western regions of the earth. It has been said that it means the Holy Land, and it has been said that it means the land of Paradise. The first is more evident. "The righteous servants" are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). So the verse contains praise of them and an announcement of a hidden matter whose fulfilment appears in existence, since Allah opened the eastern and western regions of the earth to this community.

This is an address to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and it contains great honor for him. The word *rahmah* (mercy) is in the accusative because it is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) of the object pronoun in the verb. On this reading the meaning is that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is the mercy. It may also be a verbal noun in the accusative as a *hal* of the subject pronoun, with the sense: "We sent you as one showing mercy to the worlds." Or it may be a *maf'ul li-ajlihi* (object of purpose), with the sense: "We sent you for the sake of mercy to the worlds." In every case the meaning is that God showed mercy to the worlds by sending our master Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, because he brought them the greatest happiness and deliverance from the greatest wretchedness. Through him they gained many goods in this world and the next. After ignorance he taught them, and after misguidance he guided them.

If it is said: "*Rahmah lil-'alamin* (a mercy to the worlds) is general, yet the disbelievers were not shown mercy by him?" The answer has two parts. First, they were positioned to receive mercy through him had they believed, so it was they who forfeited the mercy after it was offered to them. Second, they were shown mercy through him in that they were not punished with the like of what befell the earlier disbelievers, such as the flood, the Cry, and similar punishments.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 21, verses 109–112:**

﴿I have announced to you on equal terms﴾ meaning: I have informed you of the truth on an equal footing in the announcement and delivery, to all of you, without it being singled out for one person over another.

﴿And I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ Here, and in the other place, "in" (إن) is negative, and "adri" (أدري, I know/I do not know) is a verb suspended (muʿallaq) from its object, because it is one of the verbs of the heart (af'al al-qulub), and what follows it occupies the place of its object in meaning, so it must be connected with it. The hamza in His words ﴿aqarib﴾ (is it near) is for equalization (taswiya), not merely for interrogation. It was said that one should pause at "in adri" in both places and begin with what follows, but this is an error, because what follows it requires it (the verb needs its complement).

﴿Perhaps it is a trial for you﴾ The pronoun refers to their being given respite and the delay of their punishment. ﴿And a provision for a time﴾ meaning until death or the Resurrection. ﴿The One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ meaning: I seek His help to be patient over what you describe of disbelief and denial.
